newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African short-term interest rates at year's high.
newsitem.headline: S.African short-term interest rates at year's high.

text.p: South African short-term interest rates are at their highest level this year after rising last week as the annual year-end liquidity squeeze neared its peak, money market traders said on Tuesday.
Major banks quoted three-month negotiable certificate of deposit (NCD) rates steady at 17.40 to 17.75 percent after rising continuously towards the end of last week.
The 90-day BA rate was also steady at last Friday's high at 16.70 to 17.00 percent.

The Reserve Bank indicated the money market shortage - the amount of money the central band lends to commercial banks for their day-to-day operations - at 9.475 billion rand on Saturday from 9.499 billion rand on Friday.
Money market traders said the tight liquidity position was a short-term phenomenon and most still see a good chance of interest rates coming down in the first half of 1997.
The squeeze occurs each year in the run-up to Christmas as annual bonuses are paid out, consumers draw large amounts of money, and notes and coins in circulation in the money market system increase.

"It happens every Christmas but this particular one started too early...normally it happens from around the second week in December to the second week in January. This time it started at the end of October," one money market trader said.
The Reserve Bank quoted notes and coins in circulation at 21.971 billion rand on Saturday.
The trader said the market was quiet because players were squeezed for cash and the little cash that was around was being used to fund individual bills and was not being invested.

"Basically the guys are just trying to fight it out until January/February when they're hoping that liquidity will come off...when liquidity comes off call rates will come down and then the guys will start buying."
Behind it all lie the problems of the rand, which have deterred foreign investment in South Africa.
"The answer lies with rand. If there are rand outflows then there will be little relief," he said, adding that players were not as certain this year as they were last year of foreign investment.
Call rates are currently trading at around 18 percent.
Most traders said the outlook for next year was mildly bullish once liquidity started flowing back into the system.
"We're looking for liquidity in our system, foreign investment and a rate cut around April next year to reverse the rate hike we had in November," said one.
A recent Reuters economic forecast predicted three-month BAs would be at 15.39 percent at the end of second quarter 1997 and 14.49 percent at the end of 1997's fourth quarter.
The Bank rate currently stands at 17 percent.
